\chapter{Good Afternoon}
\label{ch:ka-good-afternoon}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can wish someone good afternoon in Kannada, and fall back on \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ} when I want a greeting that fits any hour.}

Say \kn{ಶುಭ} \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ} — built on the \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{} word rather than \kn{ಅಪರಾಹ್ನ} — and reach instead for \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}, the greeting confirmed to work at any time of day.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[śubha madhyāhna]{\kn{ಶುಭ} \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ} — good afternoon}

\label{lesson:KA-C31-shubha-madhyahna}



\begin{quote}
Two lessons ago you met a careful hedge: does \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}, \textquotedblleft{}noon,\textquotedblright{} also loosely cover \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{}? This greeting hands you a real data point.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಶುಭ} \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}} (\textbf{śubha madhyāhna}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good afternoon}\textquotedblright{} — is the standard greeting for this concept. Notice which noun it actually reuses: \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}} (\emph{madhyāhna}, \textquotedblleft{}noon,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 17) — \textbf{not} \textbf{\kn{ಅಪರಾಹ್ನ}} (\emph{aparāhna}, the word Chapter 28 established as the more precisely \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{}-specific term). This is exactly the kind of concrete usage evidence that bears on Chapter 28's own hedge: if the standard \textbf{greeting} for \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon\textquotedblright{} reaches for \emph{madhyāhna} rather than \emph{aparāhna}, that's a real (if still not fully conclusive) sign that \emph{madhyāhna}'s job has genuinely stretched to cover the afternoon in everyday use, not just at noon itself.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's the useful discipline this lesson followed: checking a claim against an actual, directly fetched source page, not just trusting a search-engine's own summary of one. That check turned up \textbf{two} claims of very different strength. \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}}'s status as a genuinely \textbf{universal} greeting — suited to any time of day, any occasion — is independently confirmed across multiple fetched sources; that one's solid. The claim that \textbf{\kn{ಶುಭ} \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}} leans \textbf{formal or semi-formal} — workplaces, official meetings — traces back to just \textbf{one} source. It's a real, directly-verified data point, worth taking seriously — but it isn't cross-corroborated the way the \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ} claim is, so treat it as a single well-checked impression, not a settled fact.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}śubha madhyāhna\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon,\textquotedblright{} reusing the \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{} word, not \textquotedblleft{}aparāhna\textquotedblright{}
  \item why that matters — real evidence for madhyāhna's meaning stretching to cover \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{}
  \item \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ} — the confirmed universal, any-time-of-day greeting, cross-checked across multiple sources
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \kn{ಶುಭ} \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ} use \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ} (\textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{}) or \kn{ಅಪರಾಹ್ನ} (the more precise \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} word)? (\textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}} — real evidence for its meaning stretching to cover \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} too.) Is the \textquotedblleft{}formal/workplace\textquotedblright{} register claim for \kn{ಶುಭ} \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ} as solidly confirmed as \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}'s universal status? (\textbf{No} — the workplace claim rests on a single directly-verified source, not cross-corroborated the way \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}'s is.) What's the confirmed universal, any-time-of-day alternative? (\textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ī]{\kn{ಈ} — one character, standing where you have only seen it riding}

\label{lesson:KA-S130-letter-ii}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಥ} — which plain letter is it built on?

One character this time. Its riding half has been on the page since your second chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಈ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಈ}} — \emph{ī}, the long \emph{i}.

By now the arrangement should be familiar, because this is the fourth vowel you have seen it in. One sound, two shapes:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಈ}} — standing alone, at the start of a word.
  \item \textbf{\kn{ೀ}} — riding on the consonant before it.
\end{itemize}

You read the riding one in the very first word you used for \textbf{you}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು}} \emph{nīvu} — you
\end{itemize}

That \textbf{\kn{ೀ}} hanging off \textbf{\kn{ನ}} is today's vowel. Pull the consonant away and it stands up as \textbf{\kn{ಈ}}.

And it has a short partner you already know, so the full square is:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಇ}} \emph{i} short, standing · \textbf{\kn{ಿ}} short, riding
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಈ}} \emph{ī} long, standing · \textbf{\kn{ೀ}} long, riding
\end{itemize}

Four shapes, two sounds, and the only questions are \emph{short or long} and \emph{standing or riding}. Notice that \textbf{\kn{ಈ}} is built out of \textbf{\kn{ಇ}} with an added stroke — the same way \textbf{\kn{ಊ}} was built out of \textbf{\kn{ಉ}}. Kannada makes the long vowel out of the short one and lets you see the seam.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಈ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{ಈ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two and say which one is the long standing vowel
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಇ}  ·  \kn{ಈ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಈ} three times, holding the \emph{ī} long as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ನೀವು} and find the riding half of today's letter inside it
  \item \emph{Say it:} the square — \textquotedblleft{}i, ī, and the same two riding\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಈ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ī}}, the long \emph{i}.) What is its riding half, and in which word have you read it? (\textbf{\kn{ೀ}}, in \emph{nīvu}.) Which short letter is its shape built on? (\textbf{\kn{ಇ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
